narr_f_walk_4: At the bottom of a narrow street behind the cathedral there's a bar with its doors open, and music coming out of it, and warm yellow light, and laughter. He goes in.
narr_bar_2: One long narrow room under dark beams. Every inch of wall is faces: portraits in charcoal and ink and watercolour, pinned up and overlapping. Old men with cigarettes. Fishermen. Children. A dog in a hat.

narr_leave_2c: The guard goes away for a long time.
guard_f_1: Nada, señor. No answer from the camp. The radio must be switched off. Perhaps they're all asleep. It's midnight.
narr_leave_2d: Alan stands by the counter with the receiver in his hand. Is it an emergency?

narr_yeray_go_2: A nice face, Alan thinks, vaguely. An unhappy face. Then he's gone into the street.

narr_q_2: They stand there in the empty bar, under the hundreds of painted faces.
rafa_upstairs: My studio's upstairs. I've got café. Real café. Not the terrible ron.
narr_q_3: Alan doesn't move. And then Rafa asks it, simply, lightly, the way you'd ask someone the time, not looking away. He's asked it before. He's the kind of man who asks.
narr_q_5: Alan thinks of a man asleep in a hotel room with one arm thrown across his chest. He thinks of the coffee by the bed. Of two small conditions, said quietly in a kitchen in Lisbon in January, as if they were nothing.
narr_q_6: Tell me first. Not after. And never to settle a fight.
narr_q_7: He thinks: he told me to go home. He thinks: he's not even answering his radio.
narr_q_8: He thinks: I'm thirty-eight years old, and I have never once stayed anywhere long enough to be left, and I'm not going to start tonight.
narr_q_9: And then, because some part of him still wants to be caught, still wants Rafa to hear it, he says it again, quieter, with a pause in front of it that anyone could have heard.
narr_q_10: Rafa looks at him for a long moment, with his head a little on one side, the way he looked at Yeray.
narr_q_11: Then he takes the pencil from behind his ear and puts it in his pocket, and takes Alan's hand in his blackened fingers, and leads him to the stairs.
narr_rafa_night_3: It's nothing like the hotel. Nothing familiar, nothing known. For an hour, in the hot dark under the roof, with Santa Ana striking the quarters, Alan is twenty-three again, and there's nothing he can lose.
narr_rafa_night_4: It's wonderful. That's the worst of it. He'd hoped, somewhere, that it would be terrible. It isn't. It's warm and real and generous and kind.
narr_rafa_night_5: Afterwards Rafa falls asleep almost at once, sprawled across the mattress like a cat in the sun. Alan lies on his back and looks at the ceiling.
narr_rafa_night_6: Through the open window, the bells of Santa Ana strike three. His family's bell among them, with his family's mark on it.
narr_rafa_night_7: The sound goes on in the dark long after the striking stops, the way a bell does, humming, remembering, and it seems to be asking him something, over and over, in a language he has always understood and always pretended not to.
narr_agustin_1: On the other side of the city, in a flat in Guanarteme two streets back from Las Canteras, a retired lifeguard called Agustín Ramos is asleep in his armchair in front of the television.
narr_agustin_2: Forty years on Las Canteras. More than two hundred people pulled out of the sea, and never one lost. There's a plaque about it at the town hall.
narr_agustin_3: What the plaque doesn't say is that in August 1958 a rip at the north end of the beach took him out past the reef and held him under, until an old man in a rowing boat got an oar to him, and then a hand.
narr_agustin_4: He has spent the rest of his life paying the sea back, one swimmer at a time.
narr_agustin_5: At three o'clock the late western on the television dissolves into grey static, and the static begins to make a sound. He knows it before he's awake: waves at the north end of Las Canteras, on a calm afternoon, past the reef.
narr_agustin_6: The carpet is wet round his slippers. Then his ankles are wet. He doesn't try to get up. He has always known, if he's honest, that this was a loan, not a gift.
narr_agustin_7: 'Thirty-eight years,' he says to the sea, quite calmly. 'You were patient. I'll give you that.'
